Description

In resting cells MEK1 and MEK2 hold inactive ERK1 and ERK2 in the cytoplasm. The N-terminal region of MEK binds ERK, and next to it MEK carries a nuclear export signal, so MEK is a cytoplasmic anchor for ERK [1]. When MEK phosphorylates the tyrosine of ERK the two dissociate, and only the freed ERK enters the nucleus [2]. Docking of ERK on MEK, beyond its phosphorylation, also governs how much ERK accumulates in the nucleus [3]. ERK leaves the nucleus again by an active route that needs MEK and its export signal and is blocked by leptomycin B, an inhibitor of the export receptor CRM1 (XPO1) [4].

References

  1. Fukuda M, Gotoh Y, Nishida E. Interaction of MAP kinase with MAP kinase kinase: its possible role in the control of nucleocytoplasmic transport of MAP kinase. EMBO J. 1997;16(8):1901-8. PMID: 9155016. doi: 10.1093/emboj/16.8.1901.
  2. Adachi M, Fukuda M, Nishida E. Two co-existing mechanisms for nuclear import of MAP kinase: passive diffusion of a monomer and active transport of a dimer. EMBO J. 1999;18(19):5347-58. PMID: 10508167. doi: 10.1093/emboj/18.19.5347.
  3. Caunt CJ, McArdle CA. Stimulus-induced uncoupling of extracellular signal-regulated kinase phosphorylation from nuclear localization is dependent on docking domain interactions. J Cell Sci. 2010;123(Pt 24):4310-20. PMID: 21123621. doi: 10.1242/jcs.076349.
  4. Adachi M, Fukuda M, Nishida E. Nuclear export of MAP kinase (ERK) involves a MAP kinase kinase (MEK)-dependent active transport mechanism. J Cell Biol. 2000;148(5):849-56. PMID: 10704436. doi: 10.1083/jcb.148.5.849.
